## Current finding

The first Predict the Self study asks whether a later Twenty Statements Test
response can be forecast from an earlier response by the same person. Its
deterministic stable-signifier projection is ready as an 81-case test
submission and passes the challenge's format validator. The private answers
remain unavailable, so this report makes no test-performance claim.

On 50 public development cases, the projection improves three of six text
agreement measures over repeating the earlier response verbatim, worsens two,
and ties one. It lowers word-count and source-similarity error but raises
line-count error. Most importantly, its mean similarity to the source is
0.903898, while observed follow-ups average 0.225683. Selecting supposedly
enduring words remains far beyond an adequate account of how people rewrite
their self-descriptions.

## How to read this report

The [evidence, method, and development results](report.html) chapter explains
the challenge for a new reader, defines the ipseological prediction target,
documents the frozen benchmark and extractive method, reports the complete
development scorecard, and links every public reproducibility artifact.

The report distinguishes three claims that should not be collapsed:

1. **Submission validity:** all 81 required IDs have nonblank predictions in
   the required order.
2. **Public development evidence:** the method has a mixed scorecard relative
   to the repeat-2024 baseline and was selected using those same public cases.
3. **Private test performance:** unknown until the organizer evaluates the
   frozen artifact; no result is inferred from validation or development data.

This Full Report is a two-chapter Quarto HTML book. Chapter count is an
editorial choice, not a Virtual CSSERG requirement.
